story.title: Netanyahu's Bloc Leads Israeli Election, But Majority Remains Elusive
story.summary: As of the latest counts, Netanyahu's right-wing bloc is leading the Israeli election but is falling short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset. With over 85% of the votes counted, projections indicate that Netanyahu's Likud party and its allies are set to secure around 53 seats, while the opposing coalition led by Eisenkot is expected to gain approximately 48 seats, alongside 19 seats for Arab-led parties. The results suggest a potential deadlock, prompting calls from President Isaac Herzog to avoid another election.

explore_lenses.label: What changed after the partial count?
explore_lenses.title: Arab parties now hold the pivotal seats
explore_lenses.summary: The notable shift is not just Netanyahu’s narrow lead: neither main bloc has 61 seats, while Arab-led parties are projected to hold 19 seats, giving them unusual leverage over whether an alternative government can survive parliamentary votes.

claims.text: At 85.6% of all ballots counted, the Central Elections Committee’s reported projection was 53 seats for Netanyahu’s bloc, 48 for Eisenkot’s bloc and 19 for Arab parties; 61 seats are required for a Knesset majority.
The count is incomplete: the committee said roughly 600,000 double-envelope ballots remained to be counted, alongside ballots requiring additional oversight.
A minority government supported in parliamentary votes by Arab parties, rather than including them in a formal coalition, is one possible arrangement described in initial reporting.

explore_lenses.label: Can either camp build a governing majority?
explore_lenses.title: Arab-party cooperation is the central obstacle
explore_lenses.summary: The arithmetic makes some form of cross-bloc or Arab-party cooperation important, but the parties’ stated conditions and objections leave the viable combinations unsettled.

claims.text: Netanyahu called for a “strong, right-wing, nationalist government” and rejected dependence on Arab parties, describing such an arrangement as dangerous; his position limits his route beyond his current bloc.

Eisenkot has said he is open to working with Arab parties only if they recognize Israel as a Jewish state and Hamas as an extremist organization; reporting indicates that some potential Arab partners have rejected those conditions.
Itamar Ben Gvir warned Netanyahu against a unity government with Eisenkot, while Eisenkot publicly accused Netanyahu of using security issues for political needs.
AP identified a Netanyahu-Eisenkot unity government and an Eisenkot-led government sustained by Arab partners outside the coalition as possible scenarios, not settled outcomes.

explore_lenses.label: What happens next under Israel’s rules?
explore_lenses.title: Herzog will consult parties after final results
explore_lenses.summary: The partial count does not itself determine the prime minister. After official results, President Isaac Herzog consults the Knesset factions and assigns a lawmaker the task of forming a government based on who appears most able to do so.

claims.text: The Central Elections Committee says final results for the 26th Knesset are to be published by November 4, 2026.

Under the Knesset’s description of Basic Law: The Government, the president assigns the mandate within seven days after official results are published, following consultations with parliamentary groups.
The first designated lawmaker has 28 days to form a government, with presidential extensions totaling no more than 14 additional days; a proposed government must then win the Knesset’s confidence.
Herzog said he expected to receive official results next week, then begin faction consultations, and urged parties to approach talks with an open mind to avoid another election.

story_report.summary: With 85.6% of ballots counted, Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc was projected to win 53 seats in Israel’s 120-member Knesset, ahead of the 48 projected for the bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot; Arab parties were projected to hold 19. Neither main bloc was on course for the 61 seats needed for a majority, leaving government formation dependent on difficult negotiations or alternative parliamentary arrangements. About 600,000 double-envelope ballots and other votes still required counting, so the estimates could change before official results.

sections.heading: Coalition Paths Face Political Obstacles
sections.body: Netanyahu called for a strong right-wing nationalist government and rejected reliance on Arab parties, a stance that limits his options beyond his existing bloc. Eisenkot has said he could work with Arab parties only if they recognize Israel as a Jewish state and Hamas as an extremist organization, conditions some potential Arab partners have rejected. Initial reporting identified a Netanyahu-Eisenkot unity government or an Eisenkot-led minority government backed by Arab parties in parliamentary votes as possible, rather than settled, outcomes.

sections.heading: Herzog Begins Government Formation Process
sections.body: The Central Elections Committee says final results for the 26th Knesset are due by November 4. After official results are published, the president is required to consult parliamentary groups and assign a mandate within seven days. The first designated lawmaker has 28 days to form a government, with possible extensions of up to 14 additional days, before any proposed government must win Knesset confidence. President Isaac Herzog has urged parties to approach talks openly to avoid another election.

unresolved.text: The final seat distribution remains uncertain until all ballot categories are counted and official results are published.

It is unresolved who will receive the first mandate and whether coalition negotiations can produce a government, including whether Arab parties would accept Eisenkot’s terms or Netanyahu and Eisenkot would consider a unity arrangement.
